analysis.one_liner: Offers House candidates full public campaign financing in exchange for small-dollar contributions and spending limits.
analysis.headline: Referred to four House committees the day it was introduced, the bill never received a hearing or vote before the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a voluntary public financing system for House elections. Candidates who collect enough small $5 contributions from voters in their state would receive public campaign funds from a new House Fair Elections Fund, cheap broadcast airtime, and extra "fair fight" money when outspent — in exchange for giving up large private contributions and personal spending. The fund would be financed by fees on broadcasters and a slice of spectrum auction proceeds, not by general taxes.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters and candidates without personal wealth or access to large donors: candidates could run competitive House campaigns funded by thousands of small $5 contributions plus public allocations, rather than courting wealthy donors and interest groups. Participating candidates would also get broadcast vouchers and discounted ad rates, and would be required to debate. The bill's stated findings argue this would reduce the influence of big contributors over legislation and free members from constant fundraising [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters and candidates without wealthy donors

how_it_helps.text: Lets any House candidate who gathers at least 1,500 five-dollar contributions from state residents opt into public campaign financing through a new House Fair Elections Fund, instead of relying on large private contributions

Gives participating candidates broadcast advertisement vouchers worth $100,000 and broadcast rates capped at 80 percent of the lowest unit charge, so candidates without big budgets can still get on the air
Provides 'fair fight funds' to participating candidates when opponents, independent groups, or electioneering spending outspend them, capped at 200 percent of their base allocation
Funds the system from spectrum auction proceeds and spectrum use fees charged to broadcasters, rather than from general tax revenue

Requires participating candidates to hold public debates and subjects them to random audits of at least 30 percent of participating committees each cycle, while imposing new reporting on nonparticipating opponents
Bans taxpayer-funded congressional mass mailings (franked mail) by members who are running for re-election during the 90 days before primary and general elections

analysis.who_pays: Broadcasters: TV and radio stations would pay a spectrum use fee of 2 percent of their gross advertising revenues each year, must accept vouchers and give participating candidates steeply discounted, non-preemptible ad time, and face possible license revocation for refusing candidates access — costs that would otherwise not exist and that stations might pass on to advertisers. The Treasury also gives up a 10 percent share of recovered spectrum auction proceeds that currently flows to it. Large campaign donors and interest groups would lose their channel of influence over any candidate who opts in [S2] [S3].

drawbacks.text: The program is funded by a 2 percent annual fee on broadcasters' gross advertising revenues and by redirecting 10 percent of recovered spectrum auction proceeds — money those industries would otherwise keep and the Treasury would otherwise receive — and broadcasters could pass the fee on to advertisers and, ultimately, consumers

Participation is voluntary, so candidates who can raise big money or benefit from heavy outside spending can simply stay out, and 'fair fight' matching payments can escalate total campaign spending rather than reduce it

The ban on franked mass mailings in the 90 days before elections restricts a communication channel members use with constituents, which critics view as tying public campaign money to limits on official speech
The bill covers only House races, leaving Senate and presidential campaign financing untouched

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real public money — collected from broadcasters and spectrum auctions rather than income taxes — spent on political campaigns, in exchange for severing candidates' dependence on large private checks. The design is more careful than a simple subsidy: it requires demonstrated small-dollar support (1,500 $5 contributions), imposes debates, audits, and repayment penalties, and covers only House races. But because participation is voluntary and outside spending is only partially offset by matching funds, the bill would not fully remove big money from House elections, and its funding mechanism leans on a single industry. Still, the principal benefit — candidates answerable to thousands of small donors instead of a few large ones — would have gone to ordinary voters.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to four House committees on the day it was introduced and died there when the Congress ended, without a hearing, markup, or vote.

narrative.text: Rep. John Larson introduced the Fair Elections Now Act on September 23, 2008, joined by Rep. Walter Jones of North Carolina as the bill's only cosponsor

That same day, the House referred the bill to four committees — House Administration, Energy and Commerce, Oversight and Government Reform, and Rules — and to the Subcommittee on Telecommunications and the Internet
No committee ever reported the bill, and the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 with no hearing, markup, or floor vote recorded

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent members' existing fundraising operation, large donors, and broadcasters, who avoided the 2 percent spectrum fee and discounted ad rates the bill would have imposed; the private financing system the bill criticized stayed exactly as it was.

for.name: Rep. John B. Larson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Fair Elections Now Act in September 2008 and assembled its provisions on public financing, broadcast vouchers, and spectrum fees

for.name: Rep. Walter Jones
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making it bipartisan on paper with one Republican supporter

against.name: House committee leadership
against.role: Chairs of the House Administration, Energy and Commerce, Oversight and Government Reform, and Rules Committees
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never held a hearing or reported it, leaving it to die when the Congress ended

against.name: House leadership
against.role: Speaker and House majority leadership, 110th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor or scheduled any action on it during the final months of the Congress

sides.party_line_note: No committee or floor votes were ever recorded; the only recorded support was the Democratic sponsor and a single Republican cosponsor, so the partisan shape of the House as a whole was never tested.

industries.note: Stations would pay an annual spectrum use fee of 2 percent of gross advertising revenues, sell participating candidates airtime at 80 percent of the lowest unit charge, accept government vouchers as payment, and lose the ability to preempt paid candidate ads — with license revocation possible for denying access. Their advertising costs would rise and their pricing power over political ads would shrink.

industries.industry: Large campaign donors and special-interest PACs
industries.note: Any House candidate who opts into the program must refuse contributions beyond small seed-money and $5 qualifying contributions, cutting off the large-dollar giving channel through which donors and PACs currently build access to House members. Nonparticipating opponents would also face new 48-hour reporting of totals once they spend heavily.

The voucher program and rate caps would redirect political ad dollars into a regulated channel with standardized FCC reporting of ad buys, shrinking the premium rates and opaque pricing that currently benefit media consultants and stations during campaigns.
